mcqs.question: In a trace waterfall, the API gateway's span contains a nested span for its call to the inventory service. What does this parent-child relationship represent?
options: That inventory is a more important service than the gateway
That the inventory call happened chronologically before the gateway span started
That the two spans belong to unrelated requests, shown together for convenience
That the inventory call is a unit of work that happened inside, and is timed relative to, the gateway's overall handling of the request
mcqs.explanation: Parent-child span nesting shows that the child (inventory call) is timed within the parent's (gateway's) span, which is exactly what lets a waterfall show which nested call ate most of the parent's total duration. It's not about importance, doesn't imply the child ran before the parent started, and both spans belong to the same trace, not unrelated requests.

mcqs.question: A service publishes a message to a queue using a raw client instead of the standard tracing-instrumented HTTP library. What's the risk?
options: The queue consumer will silently receive the message without the trace context, breaking the trace at that point without any error
The message will fail to publish entirely
Tracing will automatically detect and patch the missing context
The message will be delayed until the trace context is manually added
mcqs.explanation: Context propagation depends on every hop explicitly forwarding the trace context; a raw client that bypasses the instrumented library won't do that automatically, so the consumer gets no trace context and the trace silently splits, with no error raised anywhere. Tracing libraries don't auto-detect and patch gaps, and there's no publish failure or delay involved.

mcqs.question: Why might tail-based sampling catch a rare failure that head-based sampling at 1% misses entirely?
options: Tail-based sampling traces every request regardless of outcome

Head-based sampling decides whether to trace a request before it runs, so a rare failure has only a 1% chance of being sampled at all; tail-based waits until the request finishes and can choose to keep it because it was slow or errored
Tail-based sampling is simply a higher percentage rate than head-based by definition
Head-based sampling only applies to successful requests
mcqs.explanation: Head-based sampling commits to trace-or-not before the outcome is known, so a rare 1-in-10,000 failure has only a 1% chance of being one of the sampled requests. Tail-based sampling defers the decision until the request completes, letting it selectively keep exactly the errored or slow ones. It's not about a fixed higher rate, and head-based applies to all requests, not just successes.

mcqs.question: A team wants to reliably catch rare production incidents without paying to trace 100% of traffic. What sampling strategy fits best?
options: 100% head-based sampling, accepting the full overhead cost
0% sampling, relying entirely on metrics and logs instead
Low-rate head-based sampling plus tail-based sampling that keeps errors and high-latency requests
A fixed 50% sample rate applied uniformly regardless of outcome
mcqs.explanation: Combining a low, cost-controlled head-based baseline with tail-based sampling for errors and high latency gets the debugging value of catching rare incidents without the cost of tracing everything. Tracing nothing loses the localization traces provide, tracing 100% is the expensive extreme being avoided, and a flat 50% rate ignores outcome, so rare failures can still be missed by chance.

mcqs.question: A legacy service in the request path doesn't forward the traceparent header. What actually happens to the trace, and how would you notice?
options: The whole request fails with a tracing error, making it easy to spot immediately
The trace silently splits into two disconnected traces at that service, with no error raised — you'd only notice by specifically trying to follow a request through that exact hop
The tracing system automatically stitches the trace back together using timestamps
Nothing changes, since header propagation is optional metadata with no effect on tracing
mcqs.explanation: Dropping the trace context doesn't raise any error — the request still succeeds, but the trace silently splits into two disconnected pieces at that service, invisible until someone tries to follow a request through exactly that hop. There's no automatic timestamp-based stitching, and propagation isn't optional if you want one connected trace.

mcqs.question: A trace waterfall shows a child span apparently starting slightly before its parent span, and an on-call engineer suspects the instrumentation is broken. What's the more likely explanation?
options: Clock skew between the two services' local clocks, distorting the raw timestamps rather than reflecting a real ordering problem
The tracing library definitely has a bug that must be patched immediately
Parent spans are always required to start after every one of their children
This can only happen if the two services are in different data centers
mcqs.explanation: Small clock disagreements between machines are common even with NTP running, and they can make timestamps look impossible without any real bug in the instrumentation or the actual request flow. It isn't necessarily a library bug, parent-child ordering is logical rather than strictly timestamp-enforced, and this can happen even between services in the same data center.
